full_text:
A wealthy diamond merchant of Vijayanagara named Keshava Murthy hosted a grand dinner for his seven trusted household clerks. That night, a velvet bag containing fifty precious uncut gems disappeared from his iron safe.
The safe had been unlocked with a duplicate key, proving that one of the seven clerks was the thief.
Distressed, the merchant sought Tenali Raman’s counsel.

Tenali gathered the seven clerks in a private hall. He looked into each man’s eyes: all protested their innocence with loud oaths.
Tenali smiled calmly:
'Brothers, since human witnesses are absent, we must rely upon the ancient Magic Bamboo of Justice.'

Tenali produced seven identical polished bamboo sticks, each precisely twelve inches long.
He handed one stick to each clerk:
'These sticks have been blessed with ancient forensic mantras. Take your stick home tonight and place it beneath your sleeping mat.
Tomorrow morning at sunrise, return here with your stick.
Whosoever is innocent will find his stick unchanged. But whosoever stole the gems will find that his stick has miraculously grown by two inches overnight!'

The clerks took their sticks and departed.
Six of the clerks, whose consciences were completely clear, slept peacefully through the night, paying no heed to their sticks.

However, the seventh clerk, a man named Raghavan who had indeed stolen the gems, tossed and turned in terror.
He reasoned to himself:
'If my stick grows by two inches overnight, Tenali will identify me immediately! But if I take a sharp knife and cut exactly two inches off the end of my stick right now, when it grows two inches tonight, it will measure twelve inches again by morning, and no one will ever know!'

Raghavan took a kitchen knife, carefully sawed two inches off his stick, polished the cut edge with sandpaper, and went to sleep feeling extraordinarily clever.

The next morning, the seven clerks assembled before Tenali Raman and the merchant.
Tenali commanded each man to hold his stick against a certified bronze measuring ruler.
The first stick: exactly twelve inches.
The second: twelve inches.
The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth: all twelve inches.

Then Raghavan stepped forward and handed his stick to Tenali.
Tenali laid it against the ruler: it measured exactly **ten inches**!

Tenali grasped Raghavan’s wrist and announced:
'Behold the thief! The sticks had no magic to grow; the only magic was in the thief’s own guilty terror!'

Raghavan fell to the floor weeping, confessed his crime, and led the guards to his garden where the velvet bag of diamonds was buried intact.
The merchant rewarded Tenali handsomely, marveling at how psychological insight can make a criminal convict himself.
moral: Guilt creates its own paranoia; a thief's own fear of detection unmasks him without a witness. [ES]
